cells.tense: The thinking is moving now, and it is moving at the right speed.
cells.ask: Say the one reason you already trust, out loud, before explaining it to anyone.
cells.core: There's a way you strip a problem down to the one thing in it that's actually true. Not by being loud — by finding the thread in a pile of half-thoughts and setting it out where it can be seen. People get clearer near you, and they tend to say so. That part is running well right now.\n\nWhat this balance can feed next is showing it. The same clear eye that takes bad ideas apart can carry a finished thought you're glad to have. It doesn't have to be an argument. Put the thing you actually see in the room, and let your own weight sit behind it. That's the version where the sharpness does the work and you get to keep the credit.

cells.verb: cutting through to what's actually true
cells.place: the room where you become what you already are

cells.tense: You are arguing a case that hasn't been put to you yet.
cells.ask: Pick the next reply you were about to give and hold it one round longer than is comfortable.
cells.core: You are running a few moves ahead. The objection is already answered in your head, the flaw is already found, the ending is already written — and the rest of the room is still arriving. The cutting is sharp, and it is early. It lands on people who were not asking to be corrected.\n\nThe steadier version of this is wanting things to make sense around you, and that's a real thing to want. It comes from being settled, not from being first. Let one round go by without you in it, and watch the ground stay under you. Then speak, and the same sharpness carries weight instead of friction.

cells.tense: You stopped trusting your own read a while back, and you have been standing behind that door since.
cells.ask: Tell one person the plain version of what you think is going on, with no caveats attached.
cells.core: The sharpness is still in there. You can feel the shape of a thing when you look at it — that part didn't go. But these days you wait, let someone else go first, keep the read until it can't misfire. The thinking stays in your head, and the room doesn't get what you see.\n\nWhat brings it forward isn't forcing yourself to be clever. It's talking with someone about something that matters to you — not to win, just to hand over what you noticed. When you pass meaning to a person who is listening, the thinking starts moving again on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You have the read. You have stopped saying it.

cells.tense: You are already cutting through the confusion, and you are calling it something else.
cells.ask: Name one thing you made clear for someone today and give yourself the credit for it.
cells.core: You are the one who makes it make sense. Someone comes to you tangled and leaves with a thread they can hold, and afterward you file it under just talking, or just asking questions, or just being around. But finding the thread and pulling it — that was yours. You did that.\n\nSo hand yourself the credit that goes with it. Not as a boast, just as a fact that happens to be true. When someone says you helped, take it, and let it land where it actually came from. That keeps the clarity attached to the one doing it instead of letting it drift off as if it happened on its own.
